{{Short description|Indefinite quadratic forms in > 4 variables over the rationals nontrivially represent 0}}
{{For|the theorem in computational complexity theory|P/poly}}

In [[number theory]], '''Meyer's theorem''' on [[quadratic form]]s states that an [[indefinite quadratic form]] {{Mvar|Q}} in five or more variables over the [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[rational number]]s nontrivially represents zero. In other words, if the equation {{Math|1=''Q''(''x'') = 0}} has a non-zero [[real number|real]] solution, then it has a non-zero rational solution. By clearing the denominators, an [[integer|integral]] solution {{Mvar|x}} may also be found.

Meyer's theorem is usually deduced from the [[Hasse–Minkowski theorem]] (which was [[mathematical proof|proved]] later) and the following statement: 

: A rational quadratic form in five or more variables represents zero over the field {{Math|&Qopf;<sub>''p''</sub>}} of [[p-adic number|''{{Mvar|p}}''-adic numbers]] for all {{Mvar|p}}.

Meyer's theorem is the best possible with respect to the number of variables: there are indefinite rational quadratic forms {{Mvar|Q}} in four variables which do not represent zero. One family of examples is given by 

:{{Math|1=''Q''(''x''<sub>1</sub>,''x''<sub>2</sub>,''x''<sub>3</sub>,''x''<sub>4</sub>) = ''x''{{su|p=2|b=1}} + ''x''{{su|p=2|b=2}} &minus; ''px''{{su|p=2|b=3}} &minus; ''px''{{su|p=2|b=4}}}},

where ''{{Mvar|p}}'' is a [[prime number]] that is congruent to 3 [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] 4. This can be proved by the method of [[infinite descent]] using the fact that, if the sum of two [[square number|perfect squares]] is divisible by such a ''{{Mvar|p}}'', then each summand is divisible by ''{{Mvar|p}}''.
